# A Field Guide to the Marginal Fauna of Unfinished Books

*For use with abandoned manuscripts, interrupted journals, and novels whose authors have gone downstairs and not yet returned.*

Before examining a specimen, determine whether the book is truly unfinished. A completed book left unread supports an entirely different ecology, chiefly silverfish and resentment.

Use indirect light. Never shake the spine. Several marginal species interpret this as courtship.

## 1. The Errant Comma
*Virgula ambulans*

**Appearance:** A glossy, black-bodied invertebrate, usually 1–3 millimeters long, with a hooked abdomen and one minute foot. At rest it is indistinguishable from ordinary punctuation, except that its shadow falls toward the lamp.

**Habits:** Errant commas graze on the pauses between words. By day they shelter beside subordinate clauses; at night they migrate into the margins to molt. Their discarded skins resemble apostrophes and are responsible for a disproportionate number of possessive errors.

They are social but not cooperative. A colony will spend several hours arranging itself into a semicolon, then disperse when asked to bear any structural weight.

**Telltale marks:** Sentences that acquire a hesitant quality overnight. Small black crescents near the gutter. A faint ticking when the book is closed.

**Field note:** Do not attempt to correct them with a pen. The added ink fattens them.

## 2. The Thimble Fawn
*Cervulus minimus*

**Appearance:** No larger than the bowl of a teaspoon, with a translucent body and ears made of the soft fibers that rise from worn paper. Its antlers are two unfinished pencil strokes. Through its chest, one can see a heart the color and size of a printer’s registration dot.

Newborns have no hooves. They must be carried across the page by an adult until their first full stop hardens.

**Habits:** Thimble fawns nest beside sentences the author liked but could not find a place for. They sleep standing in the indentation of a paragraph, trembling slightly whenever a distant chapter is deleted.

When startled, a fawn attempts to hide behind the nearest capital letter. This is rarely adequate. It will nevertheless close its eyes and wait very politely to become invisible.

In cold manuscripts, it brings loose periods to its nest, nudging each into place with its nose. If one rolls away, the fawn follows it.

**Telltale marks:** Paired pinpricks along the lower margin; warm patches on otherwise cool paper; a word such as *small* or *home* rubbed almost illegible by repeated nuzzling.

**Field note:** A clean scrap of blotting paper makes a suitable blanket. Leave one corner folded back so the animal can find its way out.

## 3. The Parenthetical Widow
*Inclusa vidua*

**Appearance:** Usually observed as a woman seated sideways in the outer margin, knees drawn to her chest. Her height varies with the reader’s recollection of the room: witnesses describe her as either six millimeters tall or large enough that the book should not have contained her.

She has nine fingers on each hand. Her face is concealed by a thin sheet of paper bearing the reader’s name in a handwriting they recognize but cannot place.

**Habits:** The widow inhabits unfinished passages in which someone has entered a room but has not yet been described leaving it.

She waits until the reader reaches the final written sentence, then turns one page ahead.

This sound is commonly mistaken for a draft.

Do not follow it.

If observed indirectly, she appears to be sewing. Close examination shows that she is drawing a single hair through the paper, in and out, without a needle. The hair continues beyond the bottom edge of the book.

**Telltale marks:** Parentheses enclosing nothing. A damp oval on the back of a blank page. The sudden certainty that a passage has been removed, though pagination remains continuous.

In established infestations, the last sentence may change from past tense to present tense.

**Field note:** If a page contains an accurate description of what you are wearing, close the book without reading to the end of the line.

## 4. The Footnote Heron
*Ardea infra*

**Appearance:** A long-legged, ash-gray bird that stands at the base of the page with its head beneath the text. Its beak is a slender dash; its feet resemble asterisks. Mature specimens develop a collar of very small numerals.

The heron’s height is not measurable in inches. Record it instead by the number of lines it obstructs.

**Habits:** Footnote herons hunt assertions. They remain motionless below a confident statement, then strike upward with remarkable speed, extracting a qualification, an exception, or an embarrassing date.

Their calls are dry and infrequent:

*Strictly speaking.*

*Not in all editions.*

*This remains disputed.*

A territorial male can render a travel memoir impassable by noon.

**Telltale marks:** Superscript numbers with no corresponding notes. Damp, three-pointed tracks beneath the text. A bibliography containing one source nobody remembers consulting.

**Field note:** The species can be discouraged by placing a plainly unsupported claim in the index. It will stand over this for days, furious and well fed.

## 5. The Last-Line Moth
*Ultima noctivaga*

**Appearance:** Wings the pale brown of old adhesive, edged with sentences too small to read. Its body is covered in fine eraser dust. Unlike ordinary moths, it casts a rectangular shadow.

At rest, the wings form two facing pages. Neither has a page number.

**Habits:** This moth emerges only when the author has decided how the book will end but has not yet written it.

It feeds on the unwritten final line.

Feeding is slow. The moth lowers its head toward the blank paper and remains there, sometimes for years. During this period, the author may remember the ending as a tune, a landscape, or the name of someone they have never met.

When sated, the moth flies toward the nearest window. If the window is shut, it passes through its reflection instead.

**Telltale marks:** A clean, pale rectangle at the bottom of the final page. Powder on the sill, even in rooms without windows. The smell of rain shortly before anyone thinks to check the weather.

**Field note:** Do not capture a specimen in a jar. By morning, the jar will contain a perfectly ordinary moth, and you will no longer remember which book you meant to finish.

---

*Written in blue ink along the inside back cover:*

*I left the scrap of paper for the little deer.*

*It was folded neatly the next morning.*

*Tonight something much larger is trying to get under it.*

The museum occupies the ground floor of a building that was nearly a pharmacy. This accounts for the tiled walls and the faint smell of a cure.

It is open from ten until four, except on Thursdays, when it opens at ten past ten in recognition of a train.

The curator wears a gray cardigan with six buttons. There are seven buttonholes. She does not appear to be looking for the missing button.

Admission is free. A little brass dish accepts exact change.

### 1. The Glass of Water

A glass stands on a narrow shelf, its base extending three millimeters beyond the edge. Beneath it, on the floor, is a dark blue rug.

The water trembles occasionally, though the room is still.

> **GLASS THAT ALMOST FELL**  
> Kitchen of Mr. and Mrs. Bell, 17 October 1983  
>   
> Arrested by the right elbow of Mrs. Bell while she was explaining that she never interfered.  
>   
> Had it fallen, the resulting stain would have resembled Cyprus. Mr. Bell would have remarked on this. Their argument would have ended eleven minutes earlier.  
>   
> The rug has been included for geographical accuracy.

Beside the exhibit is a photograph of the Bells on holiday in Cyprus. They look disappointed by its shape.

### 2. The Speech

A mahogany lectern holds seventeen typed pages. On the first page, someone has crossed out *My fellow citizens* and written *Friends*, then crossed that out too.

A small speaker emits the sound of a man taking a breath. Every forty seconds, he takes it again.

> **RESIGNATION OF MAYOR ANTON VOSS**  
> Intended for delivery, 6 June 1951  
>   
> The mayor had resolved to confess to accepting money from the municipal paving contractor. Before he could begin, a pigeon entered the assembly chamber carrying an entire bread roll.  
>   
> Public attention did not return.  
>   
> Mayor Voss served another nine years. The paving remains poor.

The bread roll is displayed separately. Its placard identifies the donor as “a concerned bird.”

### 3. The Introduction

Two empty chairs face each other across a little table. One cup contains cold coffee; the other contains tea with a skin on it.

There is just enough room between the chairs for someone to pass carrying a suitcase.

> **MEETING OF ELENA PRICE AND DAVID MORROW**  
> Railway buffet, 22 February 1964  
>   
> Miss Price intended to ask whether this seat was taken. Mr. Morrow intended to say, “Only by my better judgment.”  
>   
> Both reconsidered.  
>   
> A subsequent marriage, three children, and a prolonged disagreement about parsley are represented here by the space between the chairs.

Visitors sometimes sit down. The curator permits this, but asks them not to introduce themselves.

### 4. The Ninth Symphony of Agnes Vale

The score rests in a glass case. There are eighty-six pages, all blank except for a sharp sign in the lower left corner of page forty-two.

Headphones hang from a hook.

> **SYMPHONY NO. 9 IN D MINOR**  
> Agnes Vale, 1908–1989  
>   
> Conceived while the composer was peeling an orange. Lost when she went to find a pencil.  
>   
> Contemporary accounts suggest a work of considerable warmth, with an unusually demanding part for the second bassoon.  
>   
> The recording lasts thirty-one minutes. Please do not mistake the silence between movements for the silence within them.

Through the headphones, you can hear someone in the next room trying to find a pencil.

### 5. The Apology

Under a bell jar lies an envelope, sealed but unstamped. The address is written so carefully that the ink has worn through the paper in two places.

> **LETTER FROM RUTH TO HER BROTHER**  
> 3 November 1977  
>   
> Begun after supper. Completed at 1:14 a.m.  
>   
> Not posted because the author could not decide whether “I was frightened” was an explanation or an excuse.  
>   
> Her brother lived four streets away for another twenty-six years.  
>   
> The museum possesses both possible replies. Neither is on display.

The envelope is warm. The curator says this is normal and asks you to stop checking.

### The Exhibit Without a Number

At the back of the museum is a square of ordinary plaster wall. A picture hook projects from it. Below the hook, a placard reads:

> **PLEASE ASK THE CURATOR.**

When you ask, she says, “No.”

If you ask what was supposed to hang there, she says, “A very small watercolor.”

If you ask why she will not explain it, she straightens one of the empty chairs in the third exhibit.

Before you leave, she gives you a postcard of the museum’s façade. It shows the tiled doorway, the opening hours, and the brass dish just visible inside. In the postcard, there is a pharmacy next door.

“Long before,” she says.

*The museum I’m going to have when I grow up.*

Beneath it is a name, and two dates, seven years apart.

The curator waits while you read them. Then she takes the postcard gently back and hangs it on the hook.

## The Museum of Unaccountable Things
*Located between Nos. 14 and 14. Open Tuesday, unless already open Monday.*

The museum consists of one room, five exhibits, and a chair reserved for the person who was just sitting in it. Admission is a small coin of a denomination you have never encountered.

### 1. The Last Inch of a Bottomless Well

A cylinder of black air stands beneath a glass bell. At its base lies a copper penny, face down. The penny can be heard arriving every eleven seconds.

**Curator’s note:** Acquired with a length of rope measuring considerably more than itself. The original bucket remains at large.

**Visitor rule:** Do not lean over the exhibit while remembering your name.

### 2. A Pair of Scissors That Cuts Things Together

Displayed open on green felt. Between the blades, two pieces of ribbon are joined by a seam that predates both ribbons.

**Curator’s note:** Formerly owned by a tailor whose trousers could not be removed from Thursday. Please disregard the small attached Thursday.

**Visitor rule:** Keep all disagreements at least six feet from the case.

### 3. The Portrait of Someone Standing Behind You

Oil on canvas, 1893–present. The subject wears a dark coat and holds one finger to their lips. If viewed against a wall, the painting becomes noticeably crowded.

**Curator’s note:** The sitter has declined identification. We have asked from both sides.

**Visitor rule:** Do not turn around to check the likeness. Complaints about the likeness must nevertheless be specific.

### 4. One Minute, Pickled

A squat jar containing a pale yellow interval, suspended in brine. Within it, a fly has almost landed on the rim of a teacup.

**Curator’s note:** Preserved at 4:17 p.m. on an otherwise undocumented afternoon. The lid is dated one minute later. The fly is not part of the collection and has repeatedly been asked to leave.

**Visitor rule:** Do not tap the glass. It is nearly finished being startled.

### 5. The Key to a Door That Has Never Existed

A small iron key hangs from a nail. Its teeth alter when no one is looking, although not into anything useful.

**Curator’s note:** Donated anonymously in a locked envelope. The envelope remains locked despite having been opened. We retain it for administrative reasons.

**Visitor rule:** If the key fits something in your pocket, leave that pocket here.

---

A narrow stair descends behind the ticket desk. At the bottom stands a locked basement door, with the following notice screwed firmly to its wood:

**NO BASEMENT BELOW THIS POINT**

**If you hear knocking, count the knocks.**  
**If the total is greater than the number you heard, notify the curator.**

**Under no circumstances admit the upstairs.**

*For use after closing. Instruments must be returned to the desk before dawn.*

### 1. Index Frost

**First sign:** The page numbers in the nearest open book begin counting backward, although no pages have turned.

**Effect on the books:** Frost forms exclusively on references to things that do not exist: demolished houses, extinct birds, cities omitted from every map. Each crystal has six arms and casts seven shadows. When the frost reaches an index, the entries alphabetize themselves by the temperature of the places they name.

**Precaution:** Place a wool bookmark at the letter M. Do not use a finger; the frost will catalog it separately from your hand.

### 2. The Low-Pressure Margin

**First sign:** A barometer left on the reference desk registers the weight of an unwritten sentence: usually between three and five grams.

**Effect on the books:** White space migrates toward the lowest shelf. Margins narrow upstairs while basement volumes swell with blankness. At the storm’s center, a single full stop remains suspended in a page-wide expanse. It attracts nearby punctuation with enough force to pull semicolons through closed covers.

**Precaution:** Close every book at a complete sentence. An unfinished clause offers the pressure system a route into the room.

### 3. Footnote Rain

**First sign:** A small superscript numeral appears above the librarian’s left shoulder.

**Effect on the books:** Footnotes fall from the ceiling at a rate of eleven per minute. They are dry until read aloud, at which point they become drops of water exactly as heavy as the facts they qualify. Unprotected books acquire sources for assertions they never made. Fiction is particularly vulnerable to corrections.

**Precaution:** Open an umbrella lined with unverified quotations. Keep it below the lamps; a footnote striking a bulb becomes an appendix.

### 4. The Returning Warm Front

**First sign:** The chair at the west window warms to thirty-six degrees Celsius. The surrounding air remains cold.

**Effect on the books:** Volumes once borrowed together lean toward one another, even across separate floors. A narrow current passes through them in the order they were read. On the desk, one book opens to page eighty-three. Its lower corner folds itself down, straightens, and folds again. The circulation ledger develops a faint indentation beneath a date from twenty-four years ago.

**Precaution:** Leave the chair where it is. Set a cup beside it, handle turned toward the window, and do not check the door.

### 5. Spine Lightning

**First sign:** Gold lettering on the shelves becomes legible with the lights switched off.

**Effect on the books:** Lightning travels horizontally along titles, jumping only between books whose last and first words can form a grammatical sentence. A complete discharge may cross forty metres without touching air. Struck volumes retain their contents but exchange the years in which they were written. Fresh ink may then appear beneath a medieval binding; a recent paperback may smell of a press dismantled in 1631.

**Precaution:** Insert one book with a deliberately ungrammatical title into each shelf. Never attempt to break the circuit with a dictionary.

**First sign:** Sound travels one shelf farther than it should. A cough beside the entrance is heard clearly in the locked atlas cabinet.

**Effect on the books:** Snow falls inside closed volumes, accumulating between pages that have never been seen. **Precaution:** Read one neglected page aloud each hour. Choose at random; the snow learns schedules.

**First sign:** The return slot clicks, and a book due tomorrow slides through it. No one is outside.

# A Field Guide to the Escapement Interior
*For clocks abandoned at least eleven years, with their pendulums still attached*

An abandoned clock does not become habitable when it stops. It becomes habitable when its remaining motion begins to repeat.

In suitable specimens, the final fraction of a second circulates between the teeth of the escape wheel. This captive interval supplies the interior with a faint, regular climate: tension rises, brass warms, tension falls, dew forms. A complete cycle takes approximately six days by an outside observer’s reckoning.

Do not wind an inhabited clock. Do not remove its hands. A loose minute hand admits drafts.

The five species below are common to temperate mantel clocks. Their abundance is not evidence that the clock could still be repaired.

## 1. Toothfelt
*Pellis dentata*

**Identification:** A low, blue-grey nap growing along the sheltered faces of brass gear teeth. Under magnification, each strand ends in a flattened disc resembling a very small thumbprint.

**Habitat:** The escape wheel and its immediate neighbours. Absent from steel components.

Toothfelt feeds on the difference in temperature between brass and the air. Its discs press flat during the warm portion of the cycle, then cup upward as the wheel cools, collecting the resulting dew.

Its peculiar adaptation is a capacity to grow only into spaces that will not be occupied by the next tooth. Even on a wheel that has remained motionless for decades, toothfelt leaves a precise clearance for the gear’s intended movement. This makes it the safest species to touch, though specimens removed from their native tooth rapidly lose their sense of direction and grow into tight, unusable knots.

Healthy colonies give off a smell like wet pennies.

## 2. Lacuna Snail
*Hiatella minuta*

**Identification:** A translucent snail, seldom larger than a screw head. Its shell contains one more chamber than can be counted.

**Habitat:** Screw recesses, empty jewel settings, and the hollow undersides of bridges.

The lacuna snail grazes toothfelt without damaging its root discs. Its rasping tongue takes only the growth produced during the current warm phase, leaving older strands untouched.

The snail’s extra shell chamber opens into an interval rather than a space. When disturbed, the animal withdraws into it and becomes unavailable for roughly three seconds. It does not turn invisible: for those three seconds, it is simply not present. Observers should resist the temptation to put a finger where it was. The snail returns at the same coordinates and cannot accommodate an obstruction.

Eggs are laid in pairs. One hatches; the other becomes the first missing chamber of the hatchling’s shell.

## 3. Counterweight Moth
*Noctua librata*

**Identification:** Narrow wings patterned like tarnished brass. The abdomen carries a dark bead suspended from a single filament.

**Habitat:** The open shaft beneath the clock face, particularly near the pendulum.

The counterweight moth cannot generate lift. Instead, it alters the weight of its suspended bead, falling upward when the bead becomes sufficiently light and descending when it grows heavy again. Its wings serve as rudders.

Adults drink dew from toothfelt. Their larvae feed on the soft inner membranes of lacuna-snail eggs, taking the egg that will not hatch. An untouched pair produces one snail; a pair visited by a larva also produces one snail. How the missing chamber is formed in the second case remains uncertain.

During courtship, two moths hang their beads from the same point on a pendulum rod. A successful pair balances there without either partner touching the metal.

The powder on their wings causes small tools to become awkwardly weighted. Handle with paper.

## 4. Oilglass Weaver
*Vitrea olei*

**Identification:** An eight-legged animal resembling a spider made from pale amber oil. Its joints are visible only when bent.

**Habitat:** Corners of the movement where old lubricant has pooled.

The weaver spins rigid threads from degraded clock oil. These threads are nearly invisible when viewed through the face of the clock, but conspicuous from behind. A mature web resembles a rack of fine glass needles.

Its prey is the counterweight moth. Rather than obstructing flight, the web catches the moth’s bead; the body continues moving until the filament draws taut.

An oilglass weaver can loosen any one joint into liquid and pass it through a narrow gap, then reform the joint on the other side. It must do this sequentially. A startled specimen therefore appears to pour itself through a crack in eight small instalments.

After feeding, it leaves the moth’s bead at the bottom of the web. These accumulations should not be mistaken for replacement bearings.

## 5. Pendulum Limpet
*Patella oscillans*

**Identification:** A black, flattened shell fixed to the rear surface of the pendulum bob. The shell’s rim is fringed with short white hairs.

**Habitat:** Exclusively the pendulum. Usually one individual per clock.

The limpet feeds on droplets of spent oil released by weavers. Its hairs strain the droplets from the air whenever the captive interval passes through the pendulum assembly.

Most of its body consists of a muscular foot capable of making one extremely small contraction per climatic cycle. This contraction moves the bob less than the width of a toothfelt strand, yet appears to prevent the circulating interval from settling permanently into any single gear.

Young limpets travel in the shells of lacuna snails. Upon reaching the pendulum, they leave during a snail’s three-second absence. The empty shell is often found adhering beside the juvenile limpet; the snail itself is rarely recovered.

Do not pry a limpet loose. Its grip strengthens as the pendulum’s weight is reduced.

## The Unclaimed Tooth

Every established colony contains one clean tooth on the escape wheel.

Toothfelt will not cross it. Snails turn aside from it. Moths approaching it increase the weight of their beads and drop. Oilglass threads fastened nearby detach within one cycle.

The clean tooth is not always the same tooth. At irregular intervals, the entire colony adopts a new one, while the former exclusion becomes ordinary habitat. The change occurs during the cool phase and leaves no visible disturbance.

Investigators have proposed a sixth organism, an impurity in the brass, or a point at which the captive interval touches time outside the case. None has been demonstrated. Scraping the tooth yields only brass. Replacing it causes another tooth to become clean.

Keep a drawing of the wheel rather than marking the tooth itself. Ink attracts snails and invalidates observations.

*The guide is wrong about the limpet.*

*I watched one leave the pendulum last night. It crossed the movement on its white hairs, inspected every tooth, and cleaned the new one itself.*

# A Field Guide to the Unsaid Forest
*Fifth edition, with corrections to the section on eye contact*

The forest begins where the old road ceases to be a road and becomes, according to the last sign, a way forward. Beyond this point, distances are unreliable but footprints are not.

Most species are shy. Several are ashamed. Collecting specimens is discouraged: removed from their habitat, they tend to become merely apt.

Carry water, a pencil, and something you have not yet decided how to say.

## 1. The Cold Shoulder
*Humerus gelidus*

**Appearance.** A solitary, roughly human shoulder, thirty to fifty centimeters across, covered in pale bark. It travels on five jointed roots. Mature specimens wear a collar of frost even in high summer. There is no corresponding head, arm, or torso.

**Behavior.** Dangerous. The cold shoulder approaches anyone attempting to leave a group and settles beside them at an apparently considerate distance. Exposure first produces numbness in the fingers, then difficulty recalling whom one might ask for help.

It cannot be driven off by shouting. Shouting lowers the surrounding temperature.

If approached, acknowledge it once and continue walking toward other people. Do not attempt to warm it with your hands. The shoulder interprets this as an invitation to stay.

**Habitat.** The outer edges of clearings; empty picnic sites; the downwind side of trees under which an argument has recently ended.

**Originating misunderstanding.** A child was told that an aunt had “given him the cold shoulder” and waited all afternoon for the other shoulder to arrive. The aunt forgot the incident. The child eventually did too. What remained learned to walk.

**Field note.** Frost on the left sleeve is diagnostic. Frost on both sleeves usually indicates weather.

## 2. The Room Elephant
*Elephas tacendus*

**Appearance.** Smaller than the familiar elephant, though still inconvenient. Its hide bears rectangular patches resembling faded wallpaper. The ears are thin plaster; the tusks have the yellow sheen of old piano keys. A faint outline of a door is usually visible on one flank.

**Behavior.** Moves only when unobserved, and then chiefly to obstruct exits. It feeds on the pauses before someone says, “Anyway.”

A room elephant can conceal itself behind a sapling provided everyone nearby agrees, without discussion, that it has done so. Photographs show it clearly. Photographers nevertheless tend to crop it out.

Calves are frequently mistaken for awkward silences until they begin damaging the furniture.

**Habitat.** Roofless cottages, abandoned meeting halls, and any clearing furnished with more chairs than its visitors require.

**Originating misunderstanding.** During a family discussion, someone asked where the elephant was. Nobody answered. Years later, when the house was demolished, the animal stepped out of the space between two load-bearing walls.

**Field note.** Do not point. This rarely improves the situation and may startle the chairs.

## 3. The Last Tunnel-Light
*Lampyris ulterior*

**Status: Critically endangered.**

**Appearance.** A narrow-bodied luminous moth, no longer than a thumbnail. Its wings are soot-colored and almost transparent. The light comes from the thorax and is warm enough to illuminate a fingertip, but not warm enough to comfort it.

In flight, the insect appears farther away than it is.

**Behavior.** Always retreats ahead of the observer. If pursued patiently, it leads to daylight. If pursued impatiently, it leads to another tunnel.

The adults live for one evening. Their eggs resemble pinpricks in darkness and may remain dormant for decades. Hatching requires a passage through which someone continues despite having ceased to expect an exit.

**Habitat.** Hollow fallen trees, fox tunnels, disused culverts. Formerly abundant in the long railway cutting at the forest’s eastern edge. None have been recorded there since the installation of dependable lighting.

**Originating misunderstanding.** A worker, hearing that there was light at the end of the tunnel, asked who was keeping it lit. No one could tell him. He left a small dish of sugar beneath the final arch every night until his retirement.

**Field note.** Never preserve a specimen in a jar. The jar becomes the tunnel, and the light goes out.

## 4. The Stoneheart
*Cor lapideum*

**Appearance.** A fist-sized mineral organism, usually gray, occasionally pink. Two chambers can be distinguished in broken specimens, though breaking them is no longer approved. Its surface is warm after rain.

It moves by contracting almost imperceptibly. A stoneheart may cross a path in eleven years.

**Behavior.** Feeds on salts dissolved in groundwater. When handled gently, it produces a slow pulse, easily confused with the pulse in the examiner’s own fingers.

Stonehearts congregate around damaged roots. Whether this benefits the trees is unknown. Saplings growing above them are notably difficult to uproot.

**Habitat.** Dry streambeds, graveled slopes, beneath benches where someone once waited longer than intended.

**Originating misunderstanding.** A woman called her brother stonehearted. After his death, she searched the ashes for something that would not burn. She found nothing, but kept searching. The first specimens were recorded beside the ash heap the following spring.

**Field note.** Those sold polished in village shops are ordinary stones. They are considerably more attractive.

**Appearance.** A dark, mobile aperture in the trunk of a living tree. At rest it resembles a knot. When open, it shows neither pupil nor iris, only a small depth in which the observer’s face appears from an unfamiliar angle.

There are no confirmed sightings of the complete animal.

The entries continue for several hundred wings.

**Day 91. The future anchor has taken our weight.**

**Day 206. Children born here do not believe anything ever turned.**

**Day 440. We have begun teaching them the sound.**

The final wing contains no date:

**Someone outside has put a hand on the winding key. Tell the sunkeeper. Tell everyone.**

It is too large to have passed through any of the surviving access holes. No seam or opening has been identified.

Inside the glass is a chair.

The chair is empty.

Every name scratched on the brass door is also scratched beneath the chair, including those crossed out.

On certain mornings there are eight names.

On others, six.

The bead has not been entered into the collection.

# A Field Guide to the Thunderstorm Library

The library appears between the first thunderclap and the first remark that the storm seems to be moving away. Its entrance is usually found where a door would be inconvenient: halfway up a retaining wall, behind a working refrigerator, on the riverward side of a bridge.

Look for a brass handle cold enough to hurt.

Inside, the weather is inaudible except in the atlases. There are seventeen reading tables, a clock displaying the correct time for somewhere that no longer exists, and a librarian who will ask you to shake out your umbrella outside, even when outside is a river.

The collection consists of things that were almost true. Mere inventions are not admitted. A book must have approached existence closely enough to leave a mark: a calculation, an envelope, a foundation stone, a second cup set out.

The following specimens are suitable for first-time visitors.

## 1. *A Practical Account of the Luminiferous Ether*

**Location:** Natural Philosophy, shelf 4  
**Binding:** Blue cloth, lightly buoyant  
**Distinguishing feature:** The diagrams move when no one is measuring them.

This edition documents an ether that was not disproved. Its properties are exact, experimentally reproducible, and faintly embarrassing. It accumulates beneath beds. Cats detect it but decline to assist.

Chapter seven describes a device that makes light travel slightly uphill. The apparatus requires copper wire, a tuning fork, and a technician who has never heard of relativity.

Do not breathe on the pages. Your breath will establish a preferred frame of reference, and the librarian will have to air the book overnight.

## 2. *Dear Mara,*

**Location:** Correspondence, drawer M–N  
**Binding:** None; twelve sheets in an envelope  
**Distinguishing feature:** The address is written in the reader’s handwriting.

The letter was composed at a kitchen table on a Tuesday, though no pen was taken from the drawer. It begins with an apology, abandons the apology on page two, and returns to it on page nine with considerably better evidence.

Mara’s identity varies. The letter does not.

Between the fourth and fifth sheets is a pressed leaf from a tree the writer intended to describe. Neither the tree nor the description was especially remarkable. This is why the leaf has survived.

The final sentence is visible only while the envelope is being closed.

Visitors frequently request a copy. Copies are available, but arrive blank. The postage is still charged.

## 3. *Municipal Timetable, Summer 2081*

**Location:** Extinct Futures, Public Transport  
**Binding:** Stapled green paper  
**Distinguishing feature:** Warm to the touch, as though carried in a coat pocket.

In this future, the city completed its tram network.

The booklet lists forty-three routes, including the Orchard Line, which served six hospitals, a public peach garden, and the district where everyone lived who had meant to leave.

Service was punctual without becoming a matter of civic pride. Nobody wrote essays about it. There were complaints about the upholstery.

A handwritten correction on page fourteen changes the last departure from 23:10 to 23:12. No other surviving document explains the delay.

If you hold the booklet to your ear, you may hear a passenger ask whether this is the right tram. Do not answer. The route depends on it.

## 4. *The Lesser Moons of Earth*

**Location:** Astronomy, oversize cabinet  
**Binding:** White leather with three circular stains  
**Distinguishing feature:** Its shadow separates into three at midnight.

An illustrated survey of the two additional moons Earth very nearly retained.

The first, **Hester**, was small, rust-coloured, and visible chiefly in the afternoon. Children were advised not to point at it during lessons.

The second, **Municipal Moon No. 2**, acquired its name after a prolonged dispute. Its principal effect was to make tides more administratively difficult.

The book includes charts for eclipses that almost happened and a photograph of three moonrises above a petrol station. On the back of the photograph someone has written: *Typical. Filled the tank yesterday.*

Open only one foldout at a time. Two will alter the water level in your glass. Three require a mop.

## 5. *Instructions for the Care of Your Father*

**Location:** Domestic Reference, restricted shelf  
**Binding:** Washable yellow boards  
**Distinguishing feature:** A shopping receipt serves as the bookmark.

This manual belongs to a future in which a particular operation succeeded.

Its advice is ordinary: change the dressing, open a window, encourage short walks, do not allow him to carry the heavy bag merely because he has announced that it is not heavy.

Later chapters cover restored appetites, unnecessary repairs to household appliances, and arguments that resume after a medically significant interruption.

The appendix contains seventeen years of suggested birthday presents. Most are socks. Three are books he already owns.

Handle this volume with dry hands. Moisture causes the shopping receipt to fade, beginning with the oranges.

## Borrowing Rules

1. **A library card may be obtained by naming something you nearly did.** The librarian does not judge its importance. “Bought a different kettle” is acceptable. False modesty is not.

2. **One item may be borrowed per storm.** Bound volumes count as one item. Letters count as one item. A complete civilisation counts as several, regardless of how neatly it is boxed.

3. **All loans are due before the thunder stops.** The date stamp is decorative. It reassures people accustomed to institutions.

4. **Do not make the contents true.** You may read, annotate in pencil, or disagree. You may not build the apparatus, send the letter, campaign for the tram, or attempt the operation. The library lends books, not permissions.

5. **Do not remove bookmarks.** Many are load-bearing.

6. **If a borrowed book begins to describe you, close it immediately.** Place it on a hard surface and inform the librarian using the phrase “There has been a shelving error.” Avoid reading ahead to see whether things improve.

7. **Renewals are possible only during the same storm.** The librarian will usually grant one if you are genuinely reading. Holding a finger between the pages while checking your telephone does not qualify.

8. **Lost books must be replaced with something equally close to having existed.** Cash is not accepted. Plans are assessed for plausibility. The librarian has heard about the café you intended to open.

At the desk there is a small saucer.

During every storm, exactly one plain biscuit appears on it. It arrives sometime after the third visitor and before the librarian notices it. No one has been seen placing it there.

The biscuit is always fresh. It has no entry in the catalogue. It leaves crumbs, weighs nine grams, and becomes soft if stored in a tin.

For eighty-one years, the librarian has attempted to determine which almost-event produced it. She has consulted unwritten recipes, unrealised wheat harvests, and the records of a bakery that missed opening by eleven minutes. Nothing matches.

Once, she left it untouched until the storm ended.

The next time the library appeared, there were two biscuits.

She now eats it promptly, standing up, with the expression of someone performing a minor but essential public duty.

# Field Notes on the Fauna and Flora of a Disused Dictionary

*Surveyed in a clothbound volume lacking its title page. The final recorded human consultation appears to have concerned the spelling of “accommodation.”*

The dictionary should be opened no more than thirty degrees during observation. Wider openings admit enough light to alter feeding behavior, and the abrupt straightening of the gutter may destroy a season’s nests.

The habitat is not uniformly dry. Humidity accumulates around words formerly spoken aloud, particularly those associated with kitchens, weather, and family relationships. Technical vocabulary is generally cooler. The plates of obsolete machinery support little beyond paper mites.

Five conspicuous species are described below. Their ranges overlap, though not always on the same page.

## 1. Margin stoat  
*Mustela marginalis*

**Identification.** A narrow, ivory-colored predator, usually the length of a semicolon. Its eyes resemble the two dots of a colon, but remain horizontal when the animal turns. At rest it can be mistaken for a crease.

**Habitat.** Outer margins, footers, and the unprinted ground beneath short entries. It avoids the gutter, where sound travels badly.

**Adaptations.** The stoat’s body compresses laterally until it is thinner than the space between paper fibers. This permits movement through closed pages, but only where the paper is blank. A printed rule is a substantial barrier; a handwritten underline is usually impassable.

Its whiskers detect interruptions in the regular vibration of type. An isolated movement among otherwise stationary letters can be located from three entries away.

**Feeding and relationships.** It hunts hinge moths during migration and occasionally takes the exposed roots of lapseflowers. Captured moths are carried into the margin and eaten from the definition outward. Their headwords are left intact.

Stoats maintain small caches of uneaten meanings. These are identifiable as pale bulges under the paper. A cache beside *shelter* contained “to keep from rain,” “a place afforded,” and part of “protection,” all still warm.

Breeding occurs in the broad margins of pages with few entries. The young remain invisible until their first kill, when a brief blood-colored dash appears behind each ear.

## 2. Lapseflower  
*Obsolescens campanula*

**Identification.** A translucent plant rooted in the final letter of an unused word. Flowers are bell-shaped, with a faint gray vein corresponding to the word’s former pronunciation.

**Habitat.** Entries whose headwords have not been read, spoken, or distinctly remembered for a prolonged interval. An “obsolete” label is neither necessary nor sufficient. Several flowers were found beneath words still marked “colloquial.”

**Adaptations.** The seed coat is impervious to dust and ordinary neglect. Germination begins only when the word’s last habitual user stops reaching for it. The distinction matters: a dead speaker’s word may remain dormant for years if someone else still remembers hearing it.

Roots enter the spaces between letters without displacing the type. They absorb the residual pressure of use, a substance most readily measured by the slight resistance encountered when turning an old page.

**Feeding and relationships.** The flower supplies hinge moths with a thin nectar tasting, by scent, of the circumstances in which its host word was once spoken. The moths distribute pollen among entries sufficiently close in meaning.

Catchword weavers collect shed petals for their nests. Margin stoats graze the roots in late winter, when moth traffic is low.

Flowering ends immediately if the headword is used correctly outside the dictionary. Misquotation causes only a temporary closing of the bells.

A stand beneath *yclept* flowered for eleven successive surveys. On the twelfth, every bloom had closed. No change in the room was recorded.

## 3. Hinge moth  
*Transitiva limen*

**Identification.** A small moth with two mismatched wings. One bears the coloring of its departure entry; the other gradually assumes that of its destination. In transit, the discrepancy is often pronounced.

**Habitat.** Cross-references, numbered senses, and definitions containing words with entries of their own.

**Adaptations.** Hinge moths follow semantic gradients rather than page order. A moth leaving *bank* may arrive at *shore*, *money*, or *tilt*. It cannot reach *banjo* merely because the entry is nearby.

The antennae are sensitive to qualifying phrases. “In law,” “formerly,” and “chiefly nautical” divert entire flights into narrow local populations. Moths trapped in circular definitions can survive indefinitely but rarely reproduce.

**Feeding and relationships.** Adults feed on lapseflower nectar. Larvae consume the fine connective material between a word and its explanation, leaving both legible but slightly farther apart.

Migration peaks shortly after dusk in the room containing the dictionary. Flights cross the gutter in single file. At exposed page edges, margin stoats take up to a third of the migrants.

There is one continuing disagreement between the researchers Vale and Sen. Vale holds that the moth’s destination is fixed at emergence. Sen has observed adults change course after encountering an unfamiliar example sentence and argues that the route is learned. Their marked specimens repeatedly arrive without their marks, so neither account has been confirmed.

## 4. Catchword weaver  
*Aranea repetens*

**Identification.** Six-legged, though four obsolete limbs can be seen folded beneath the abdomen under magnification. The body resembles a fleck of binding glue. Its silk is visible only when viewed against a word that occurs twice.

**Habitat.** Repeated headwords at the tops of pages, duplicated phrases, and the short passages between a definition and its example.

**Adaptations.** The weaver anchors its web to recurrence. Identical letters provide weak purchase; identical words provide stronger purchase; the same word used in the same sense can support a breeding female and her clutch.

A web between two instances of *light* broke when one was found to mean illumination and the other insufficient weight.

**Feeding and relationships.** Weavers intercept juvenile hinge moths and airborne lapseflower pollen. The latter is stored in silk pockets and eaten during periods when the book remains tightly closed.

They line their egg chambers with lapseflower petals, which keep the eggs from acquiring meanings too early. Unlined eggs often hatch as brief, unsuitable creatures: a verb that cannot move, a winged preposition unable to land.

Webs also provide safe crossings for index silverfish. The silverfish pay no apparent attention to the weavers, but their passage shakes loose the small prey lodged at distant anchors.

## 5. Index silverfish  
*Lepisma reperta*

# A Field Guide to the Unmeant Fauna of Lorn

*Six common species, with annotations by Dr. Ada Vale and Mr. Felix Rook.*

In Lorn, a metaphor becomes an animal when its last speaker stops meaning it.

This is not the same as forgetting. A woman may forget that she once called her husband a rock, and nothing happens. But when she remembers saying it and can no longer imagine why, something with granite shoulders climbs out of the river.

Most specimens emerge near kitchens, courtrooms, and the rear entrances of theaters. Do not feed them synonyms.

---

## 1. The Elephant in the Room
*Elephas tacitus*

**Identification:** A small gray elephant, usually between the size of a footstool and that of an actual elephant. Its dimensions depend on how much room everyone insists it is not taking up.

The ears resemble folded minutes from a meeting. The eyes are kind, which makes matters worse.

**Habitat:** Dining rooms, committee chambers, wedding receptions. Rarely outdoors; there, people tend to notice it.

**Behavior:** Feeds on pauses.

At dinner it waits beneath the table, gathering the silence between “How is your brother?” and “Would anyone like more potatoes?” with its trunk. Well-fed specimens become translucent. Through their flanks one can see the thing nobody has said, although it appears reversed, as in a mirror.

It is a sociable animal and will place a foot gently on yours whenever someone changes the subject.

**Hazards of literal handling:** Removing it from a room requires widening the door. Most households prefer to demolish the opposite wall and claim they always wanted a terrace.

Never ask, “What elephant?” It will sit in your lap.

> **VALE, margin:** Rook’s assertion that these animals feed on pauses is unsupported. The diet is plainly whole conversations.
>
> **ROOK:** I watched one eat a pause for seventeen minutes.
>
> **VALE:** You were asleep.
>
> **ROOK:** And yet you put your coat over me.

---

## 2. The Heart-on-a-Sleeve
*Cardium maniculatum*

**Identification:** A red, fist-sized animal with four fine legs and a soft, regular pulse. At rest, it looks like a velvet brooch. In motion, it looks worryingly like an organ escaping a wedding.

**Habitat:** Coat racks, laundries, the cuffs of people waiting outside apartment buildings after midnight.

**Behavior:** Attaches itself to a sleeve by means of tiny silver hooks. It is not parasitic. It merely wishes to go where you are going.

Its coloration changes with nearby speech: scarlet at compliments, blue-black at rehearsed apologies, a pale pink when someone says its name without needing anything.

During courtship, two specimens approach along opposite sleeves and exchange a single drop of warm rain.

**Hazards of literal handling:** Once attached, it becomes visible to everyone you pass. Strangers may touch it without permission. Dogs may love you suddenly.

Do not cover it with a watch. It will learn to count the seconds since a particular door closed.

To remove one safely, sit beside an open window and say something true but small. “The pears are ripe” is usually sufficient. It will unhook itself and go to investigate.

> **ROOK:** A delightful companion. Mine accompanied me through three winters.
>
> **VALE:** Yours was a scarlet mitten.
>
> **ROOK:** You repaired it twice.
>
> **VALE:** The thumb was structurally unsound.

---

## 3. The Wolf at the Door
*Canis imminens*

**Identification:** Tall, narrow, ash-colored. Its ribs resemble the slats of an empty cupboard. Its breath smells faintly of cold coins.

A reliable distinguishing feature is the brass knocker growing from its forehead.

**Habitat:** Doorsteps, especially those of buildings whose rent has recently increased. Occasionally found outside banks, where it seems confused.

**Behavior:** It never knocks.

Instead, it stands close enough that the occupants can hear its stomach through the wood. It is remarkably patient. Some individuals remain at the same door for years, aging alongside the family within.

In spring, females give birth to litters of overdue notices. These develop legs within a fortnight.

**Hazards of literal handling:** Opening the door does not make it attack. It makes it come in and assess the furniture.

Feeding it is worse. A wolf given one heel of bread will return with relatives and a modest proposal concerning your remaining bread.

It can be discouraged by leaving a light on, though this increases the electricity bill and therefore attracts it.

> **VALE:** Do not follow Rook’s advice to scratch it behind the ears.
>
> **ROOK:** Some of them have had a difficult year.
>
> **VALE:** All of them have had a difficult year. That is their anatomy.
>
> **ROOK:** There is soup in your specimen cupboard. The clean jar, not the one marked TEETH.

---

## 4. The Red Herring
*Clupea diverticula*

**Identification:** A bright red fish capable of swimming through air. Distinguished from ordinary herring by its confident expression and inability to arrive where expected.

**Habitat:** Police archives, family histories, newspaper offices. Breeds prolifically in the footnotes of unauthorized biographies.

**Behavior:** When startled, it darts toward the second-most-interesting thing in the vicinity.

A burglar may thus escape while an entire street watches a suspiciously large pigeon. In laboratory conditions, one specimen drew six researchers into a prolonged argument about whether the laboratory had always contained that particular chair.

Schools travel in intricate formations resembling arrows. These arrows point nowhere useful.

**Hazards of literal handling:** Pursuit is strongly discouraged. A red herring can lead a naturalist from a promising discovery to a suburban shed containing forty-seven commemorative mugs.

If caught, it will explain why you should have caught something else.

Its flesh tastes like an answer to a question you did not ask.

> **ROOK:** The mugs were of considerable historical interest.
>
> **VALE:** We were investigating a missing child.
>
> **ROOK:** The child was in the shed.
>
> **VALE:** By coincidence.
>
> **ROOK:** I have retained the mug you threw at me. It holds your pencils rather well.

---

## 5. The Silver Lining
*Lamina argentea*

**Identification:** A long, nearly weightless animal, part eel and part ribbon, with a skin of beaten silver. Usually visible only at the edges of dark clouds.

Juveniles resemble loose threads caught on the moon.

**Habitat:** Storm fronts, hospital skylights, the weather above canceled journeys.

**Behavior:** Grazes along the undersides of clouds, eating small holes through which light enters.

It does not prevent rain. It appears indifferent to this failure.

At dusk, several may descend to rooftop level. They pass through chimney smoke without disturbing it, and for a moment each house wears a narrow brightness, as though someone inside has lifted a lamp toward a window.

Their song is too high to hear, but glass objects lean toward it.

**Hazards of literal handling:** Never pull one free of its cloud. The cloud will fall.

A mature rain cloud weighs more than a cathedral and lands with none of a cathedral’s sense of occasion.

Nor should the animal be folded for storage. It will brighten the drawer indefinitely, and everything placed inside will look like something you ought to have kept.

> **VALE:** These sightings occur most often after exhaustion. I recommend skepticism and eight hours’ sleep.
>
> **ROOK:** You saw one over the hospital.
>
> **VALE:** I saw a meteorological irregularity.
>
> **ROOK:** You stood beneath it until dawn.
>
> **VALE:** You had not yet come out.

---

## 6. The Last Straw
*Festuca ultima*

**Identification:** A thin, golden insect with six legs, a jointed spine, and a head like a cut stalk. Commonly mistaken for litter until it begins making demands.

**Habitat:** Desks, sink drains, the space between a train’s scheduled arrival and its actual arrival.

Always found alone.

**Behavior:** The last straw selects a host already carrying too much. It then adds almost nothing.

A misplaced teaspoon. A damp sock. A cheerful recorded message.

Its weight is negligible. Its effect is not.

Before a host breaks, the insect makes a sound like one dry blade of grass moving against another. In quiet rooms, this may be audible several seconds before the shouting begins.

During winter it hibernates inside the phrase “It’s fine.”

**Hazards of literal handling:** Do not place it on a camel. This experiment has been performed. The camel survived; the researcher now lives on a houseboat and refuses all correspondence.

If one lands on you, ask another person to lift it away. This is easy for them and may be impossible for you.

Store the specimen in a spacious box. Labeling the box “miscellaneous” is prohibited.

> **ROOK:** Vale removed one from my shoulder with kitchen tongs.
>
> **VALE:** It was on your collar.
>
> **ROOK:** She then canceled my lecture.
>
> **VALE:** It was a poor lecture.
>
> **ROOK:** She told the audience I had been called away on important business.
>
> **VALE:** You had.
>
> **ROOK:** What business?
>
> **VALE:** The soup was getting cold.

---

### Note on night observation

When the tram bells stop, Lorn’s smaller fauna come out beneath the streetlights. Red herrings turn in the warm air above the gutters. Hearts climb the sleeves of coats hung to dry. Somewhere a wolf settles on a doorstep, resting its heavy forehead against the brass.

Take a notebook, a shaded lamp, and something to sit on.

> **VALE:** Also take a scarf. Rook has omitted this because he habitually loses his.
>
> **ROOK:** I have not lost it. It is the blue one you are wearing.
>
> **VALE:** Your handwriting deteriorates in the cold.
>
> **ROOK:** Keep it until we get home.

### The Universe of the Last Step

In this universe, almost everything behaves as it does here. Heat flows from hot things to cold things. Magnets have two poles. Toast is difficult to butter gracefully.

But inertia has one exception:

**Whenever a moving object comes completely to rest, it must take one additional step.**

The step is exactly one centimetre long, in the direction the object was travelling immediately before it stopped. It happens instantaneously. The object carries whatever is firmly attached to it.

Afterwards, it stays still. The extra step does not itself count as motion, so it does not trigger another step.

This last detail is important. Without it, furniture would migrate indefinitely.

---

The first scientific discovery was that stopping and slowing down were fundamentally different events.

A ball rolling very slowly across a table behaved normally. But the instant friction reduced its speed to zero, the ball shifted one centimetre farther along.

If there was empty space there, it appeared in the empty space.

If there was a wall there, it appeared one centimetre inside the wall.

Matter did not merge politely. The ball and the wall violently pushed each other apart until they no longer overlapped.

This explained why cupboards had always been built with soft backs.

The discovery became a precise law when Dr. Esme Vell stopped a bead under a microscope and found that its final displacement was the same whether it had previously been travelling at a walking pace or at the speed of an arrow.

One centimetre.

Mass did not matter. Speed did not matter. How gradually the object had stopped did not matter.

Nature apparently felt that stopping was an unfinished gesture.

### A household inconvenience

You could put a cup on a table, but you could not put it *exactly* where your hand released it.

The cup would take its last step in whatever direction you had been moving it.

Experienced people approached a placement point from one centimetre away. Inexperienced people broke things.

Worse were objects lowered vertically. A cup lowered onto a table tried to take its last step through the tabletop.

Consequently, the proper way to set down crockery was to lower it almost to the surface, slide it sideways, and then stop.

Every child was taught this.

Every visiting aunt knew a better method.

There was also the problem of washing machines. A rotating drum did not merely jump forward when it stopped: each part attempted a centimetre of travel along its own final tangent. Ordinary drums tore themselves apart.

Successful washing machines never quite stopped spinning.

They hummed gently in the night, and repair technicians approached them with the respect normally reserved for injured horses.

### What counted as an object?

This took longer to establish.

A riveted machine usually stepped as one object. A pile of sand did not. A person stepped together with their clothes, but not with a coin loosely held in an open palm.

The governing distinction was not size or material. It was mechanical attachment.

If parts were bound tightly enough to constrain one another’s motion, the whole assembly took a single step consistent with those constraints. Loose components stepped independently.

A stopped wheel therefore received an extra angular displacement: just enough rotation for its rim to travel one centimetre.

This produced the first useful technology.

A large wheel, brought repeatedly to rest, gained a little extra turn each time. The phenomenon supplied energy from nowhere anyone could identify. Scientists did not disguise this by calling it “stored.” Instruments showed that the extra movement was simply new.

The first stop-engine powered three streetlights and shredded its own bearings.

The second powered a bakery.

Within forty years, the cities were full of machines that sounded like somebody patiently failing to start a lawnmower.

### The loophole exploited by children

Adults told children that a locked door was impassable.

Children discovered that this was only approximately true.

Run toward a door. Strike it. Come to rest.

Your last step carries you one centimetre into the wood.

Normally, this is unpleasant.

But if the barrier is thinner than a centimetre, and there is enough room beyond it for your entire body, your final position contains no overlap at all. You simply appear on the other side.

The first victims were garden fences made of sheet metal.

Then school rules acquired the phrase **“including by discontinuous means.”**

Wealthy households installed doors three centimetres thick. Children responded by carrying thin boards, leaning them against locked doors, and practising.

This did not work. The entire one-centimetre displacement had to be clear at its destination; you could not accumulate progress while embedded in a solid door.

For several weeks, the children were defeated.

Then one of them noticed that a locked door might be thick, but the glass beside it was not.

Architecture changed.

### Increasingly strange examples

A projectile could pass through a thin shield if the shield stopped it cleanly enough. A thicker shield survived, although the projectile’s last step damaged its interior.

Armour therefore became either very thick or deliberately yielding. Good armour did not stop a weapon abruptly. It guided it sideways and let it come to rest facing somewhere unimportant.

A falling person, meanwhile, took their last step downward at impact.

The safest floors were deep beds of loose material. Each grain could move out of the way independently. Hospitals used foam pellets. Schools used sand. Formal dances were held on surfaces that made everyone look slightly seasick.

At the microscopic scale, the rule became stranger still.

An individual molecule could travel a centimetre when it stopped. In a gas, it seldom stopped exactly; collisions usually left it moving in another direction. But a molecule captured by a cold surface took its last step into—or through—that surface.

Very thin containers leaked in a peculiar fashion.

Very thick containers were gradually damaged from within.

The reliable way to imprison a gas was to keep its molecules moving.

This was not especially difficult until somebody wanted to study absolute zero.

Their apparatus became the first object in history to escape from a locked laboratory without having any moving parts.

Then astronomers found the same rule in orbit.

At the farthest point of a highly elongated orbit, a body slows, but does not stop. It gets no step.

A body falling directly toward a star, however, can be brought momentarily to rest by radiation pressure. It then takes a centimetre toward the star before being pushed back.

Under the right conditions, dust grains repeatedly approach, halt, step, and retreat.

There are stars surrounded by enormous, faintly luminous shells of dust that can never quite leave and never quite arrive.

From a distance, these stars look ordinary.

Up close, their halos sound like sleet tapping on a window.

### The expedition to the edge

Eventually someone asked whether the rule could cross the boundary of the universe.

The universe was small enough to have an edge: a perfectly black surface that no light penetrated and no force displaced.

An expedition built a vehicle with a crushingly effective brake. They approached the boundary, stopped with the front of the vehicle one millimetre away, and waited for the last step.

The vehicle did not enter the darkness.

It moved one centimetre sideways.

They tried again.

Again, sideways.

They approached from different angles. They tried individual beads, arrows, living volunteers, a very nervous goat. Every object took exactly one centimetre, but always in a direction that kept it inside.

The rule had previously been understood as:

> Continue one centimetre in your last direction of motion.

It was now revised:

> Continue one centimetre in your last direction of motion, unless that direction is unavailable.

Which sounded reasonable until you asked how an instantaneous step could discover that a destination was unavailable.

The leading theory was that it did not discover anything. Perhaps every object had already made its last step, and ordinary motion was merely catching up.

Nobody liked the mathematics of this.

The goat refused to approach the boundary again.

### The unanswered question

Here is the question nobody has managed to answer:

**Does the universe itself have a last step?**

There is no agreed way to determine whether the universe is moving. There is no agreed place for it to stop. There is certainly no agreed direction for it to go afterwards.

Nevertheless, a small observatory near the edge maintains a permanent watch.

Its floor turns very slowly beneath the astronomers’ chairs, so that the building is never entirely still.

This is not thought to help.

It just makes the astronomers feel better.

My father made doors that went nowhere.

He worked in the shed, shaving pale curls from the wood. I swept them into sacks while he fitted the hinges. When a door was finished, he stood it upright without a wall and knocked.

Something always knocked back.

“Customer,” he’d say.

“Who?”

“Nobody.”

This was his only joke. Among door-makers, it was considered filthy.

Most people wanted doors to somewhere: a sister’s kitchen, the seaside, the summer before their knees went bad. My father refused those commissions. He built narrow doors with plain brass handles, and charged almost nothing.

Once, when I was nine, I looked through the keyhole.

There was a beach without a sea. A single shoe stood at the edge of the sand, patiently, as if waiting for its other foot.

My father covered the keyhole with his thumb.

“Not yours,” he said.

After he died, I found an unfinished door beneath a sheet in the shed. Its handle was wrapped in cloth. I unwrapped it, and the brass left a cold, penny-shaped smell on my palm.

I knocked.

Nobody answered.

I knocked again, harder.

“Oh, come in,” said my father. “You’ve never needed an invitation before.”

Beyond the door was a small room furnished with things we had lost. The blue bowl I broke at eleven sat whole upon a table. His wedding ring lay beside it, still trailing the bit of string he’d tied around it when his fingers grew thin.

My father was trying to mend a kite.

“You’re dead,” I said.

“Yes. Could you hold this?”

I took the bamboo spar. He wound thread around the joint, pulling it tight with his teeth.

“Is this nowhere?”

“Part of it.”

“Can you come home?”

He glanced at the door. Through it I could see the shed, the empty chair, the sheet collapsed on the floor.

“I don’t think so.”

We finished the kite. There was no wind in the room, but it rose when he let go, tugging gently at the string.

When I turned to leave, I noticed another doorway behind his chair. Beyond it stood a woman holding an unbroken blue bowl. She lifted her head at the sound of my voice.

My father had made her a door, too.

I had always thought nowhere was where his doors went.

It was where they came from.
